title: Autofailover signal classifier and tier-aware throttling orchestrator
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: Implement a robust, explainable signal classifier and orchestrator that triggers automatic failovers and tier-aware throttling across regions and model variants. This ticket covers the algorithmic ruleset, runtime integration points, safe defaults, and integration tests for detecting congestion (429s), latent queues/timeouts, and correlated error-rate spikes, then invoking appropriate mitigations: regional reroute, tier downgrade, model-variant swap, or progressive backoff.

Scope:
- Define a compact signal model (inputs: 429 rate, 5xx rate, per-request latency percentiles, inflight queue depth, token-rate exhaustion signals) and a priority-weighted scoring function that is interpretable and tunable by SRE/PM.
- Implement a stateful per-route 'orchestrator' that keeps short-lived hysteresis windows (300-1200s) and enforces cooldowns, per-customer overrides, and telemetry tags.
- Add tier-aware actions: soft-throttle (rate-limit at route level), degrade to lower-cost tier model variant (quantized model), route to alternate region, or open a controlled circuit (reject-fast with structured error and fallback hint).
- Safety: add phased rollout (canary on non-critical routes), rate-limited automated actions, and manual abort hooks in Console.
- Observability: new metrics, alert rules, and a debug trace that explains why a decision was made (input signals -> score -> action).

Acceptance criteria:
- Deterministic unit tests for classification logic and interval hysteresis.
- Integration test that simulates 429/timeout flood and verifies orchestrator issues the expected action within SLO (<=2x decision window).
- Console shows event history and rationale for any automated action.
- Runbook updated and owners assigned.

Trade-offs/Notes:
- We intentionally prefer a lightweight, rule-based classifier over an ML model for predictability and immediate explainability in incidents. This can be iterated into a statistical model later once we have historical labeled data.
- Per-customer overrides increase complexity but are necessary for enterprise SLAs; initial MVP exposes allow/deny lists and a severity multiplier rather than full policy language.
